subject_entity.title_display: Book of the Laws of Countries
subject_entity.notes: Dialogue attributed to Bardaisan of Edessa (c. 196); defends human free will against astrological determinism; argues that diverse human customs across nations disprove fate; the earliest surviving Syriac literary composition.

object_entity.notes: Syriac philosopher-theologian born in Edessa; wrote the Book of Laws of Countries defending free will against fate; initially associated with Valentinian Gnosticism per Eusebius HE 4.30 but later opposed it; founded an influential school at Edessa; refuted by Ephrem.

evidence.notes: This passage from the work attests its existence and authorship.

passage.locator: Book of Laws of Countries (central argument)
passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Bardaisan catalogs the diverse laws and customs of nations — Brahmins in India, Persians, Britons, Chinese — demonstrating that human behavior differs by culture, not by zodiac; if fate determined all, customs would be uniform; therefore free will prevails over astral determinism.

evidence.notes: Addressed to Roman governors of Carthage province; describes local community

passage.excerpt: We are a body knit together by a common religious profession, by unity of discipline, and by the bond of a common hope. We meet together as an assembly and a congregation. We pray together, we read scripture, we offer exhortation. Our presidents are elders, approved men. There is no buying and selling of any sort in the things of God. Even if there is a chest of sorts, it is not made up of purchase-money. On the monthly day, each puts in a small donation, if he will, and only if he be willing; for no one is compelled. These gifts are not spent on feasts or drinking bouts but to support and bury poor people, to supply the wants of boys and girls destitute of means and parents, and of old persons confined to the house.
passage.notes: Description of Christian assembly, common fund, and community life in Carthage

subject_entity.notes: Tertullian's early treatise on repentance c. 198-200; allows one post-baptismal repentance through church discipline; important early witness for penitential practice.

object_entity.notes: First major Latin Christian author; active in Carthage c. 195–220. Wrote at least 31 works spanning apologetics, anti-heretical polemic, and moral discipline. Coined 'trinitas' and 'tres personae una substantia'. Defender of apostolic succession, rule of faith, incarnation, and bodily resurrection. Later attracted to Montanist rigorism c. 207; teacher of Cyprian by doctrinal influence.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Tertullian teaches that after baptism, God has provided one further repentance (exomologesis) for those who fall into grave sin. This second repentance is a painful public confession before the congregation, including fasting, weeping, and prostration; it is the last remaining refuge for the sinner, but it does exist.
passage.notes: One post-baptismal repentance allowed through exomologesis (public confession); early penitential discipline
